title: Coverage cliff: past DENSE_LIMIT the only route gives Ha-scale widths
description:
certkit-jn1.1/jn1.3 finding, now quantified on real molecular Hamiltonians via the Pauli backend:

  case  dim   route                width      chemical accuracy
  H2     16   temple_inertia       3.7e-09 Ha   ok
  H2     16   gershgorin_rayleigh  1.6e-01 Ha   100x too wide
  H4    256   gershgorin_rayleigh  7.9e-01 Ha   500x too wide
  N2   4096   gershgorin_rayleigh  2.6e+00 Ha   1600x too wide

Every one of these VERIFIES and every one contains the exact value, so soundness is intact and this is purely coverage. But past n = 160 the inertia route is gone, so the gap cannot be discharged, so Temple cannot be used, and the only surviving route is a Gershgorin floor whose width grows with the operator. Chemical accuracy is 1.6 mHa. Nothing above 16 dimensions is within three orders of magnitude of useful.

This is the concrete case for the README's 'a count rule that works matrix-free' item: it is what would let a large Pauli Hamiltonian use temple_ref instead of falling back to Gershgorin, and it is the difference between certkit being a demonstration and certkit being usable on the Krylov solver's real workloads.
acceptance_criteria: A counting rule that discharges the gap hypothesis without an O(n^3) dense factorisation, giving a Temple-quality width on a Pauli-sum operator of at least 256 dimensions.

Closed the one concretely-named door session 5 flagged as untried: a
fill-reducing SPARSE (non-banded) LDL^T elimination order for PauliSumReal,
as opposed to the banded route's fixed-bandwidth failure.

Key structural fact: a PauliSumReal term with nonzero bit-flip mask m
connects basis state i to i^m for every i, so the operator's sparsity graph
is exactly the Cayley graph on Z_2^q generated by the term masks. For a
TFIM-shaped Hamiltonian (one X per qubit, e.g. examples/sample/pauli_operator.json)
this is exactly the q-dimensional hypercube Q_q.

Result 1 (closed form): removing the single Hamming-weight layer L=q//2
disconnects {weight<L} from {weight>L} -- a constructive balanced separator
of size C(q,q//2), verified as a legitimate cut computationally for q up to
24. sep/n shrinks only as 1/sqrt(q) (Stirling), i.e. polylog in n -- nowhere
near the O(sqrt(n)) separators (planar/mesh graphs) nested dissection needs
to give genuinely sub-cubic factorization.

Result 2 (direct measurement, not just the bound): ran greedy minimum-degree
symbolic elimination (the standard practical fill-reducing heuristic,
what CHOLMOD/SuiteSparse actually use) on real sparsity graphs -- pure TFIM
hypercube AND a JW two-body chemistry-shaped case (reusing session 5's
from-scratch JW transform), q/M = 4..12, n up to 4096. Tracked fill edges
and an op-count proxy (sum of pivot-degree^2, same cost model banded.py's
O(n*b^2) claim uses). ops/n^3 CONVERGES TO A CONSTANT across three doublings
of n in both cases (~0.026 TFIM, ~0.08 JW) rather than shrinking -- confirms
Result 1's prediction with an actual solver's output, not just a bound.
max_deg also grows linearly in n (~0.4-0.5n), consistent with the slow
separator shrinkage.

Conclusion: minimum-degree fill-reducing ordering does not change the
GROWTH ORDER of LDL^T cost for PauliSumReal -- only a roughly constant
13x-38x reduction vs. literal dense O(n^3) in the tested range, and the
separator argument says that constant does not keep improving past what

title: Krylov sector scope does not survive translation to lambda_min_enclosure
description: certkit-jn1.1 finding. The solver's Temple bracket is certified against the lowest REACHABLE levels (temple_bounds.py honest-scope note); certkit's lambda_min_enclosure is a claim about the whole operator. Transcribed directly for H2/sto-3g the self-mode eps = -0.2320 Ha while the matrix's true lambda_2 = -1.2533 Ha, so the Temple premise eps <= E_1 fails by 1.02 Ha and the checker refuses: '13 eigenvalues lie below beta, need exactly 1'. Here the sector ground happened to coincide with the global lambda_min so the CLAIM was still true and only the PREMISE was wrong. On a molecule where a lower-lying sector exists, the same translation emits a claim that is false, not merely unproven.
acceptance_criteria: Either a sector-restricted claim kind that carries its subspace as part of the claim, or a documented producer rule that beta must separate the full spectrum and a full-space route for obtaining it.
notes:
RESOLVED. Constructed the deliberate adversarial case the prior notes asked
for: tests/test_sector_scope.py builds a 5-dim block-diagonal operator with
two decoupled sectors, where sector A's local ground/gap (self-mode eps=-1.0,
beta=1.0, mirroring the H2 case's shape) is NOT the global minimum (sector B's
ground is -4.0). A hand-built certificate submits exactly what a naive bridge
would: sector A's exact local eigenvector and local beta, translated directly
into a lambda_min_enclosure claim on the whole operator -- a *point* claim
[-1.0, -1.0], as confident as a false claim can look (residual is exactly 0
since the vector is an exact eigenvector of the block-diagonal operator).

check() abstains: "2 eigenvalues lie below beta, need exactly 1." Confirmed
this isn't magnitude-dependent (a 0.01 violation is still caught, not just
H2's dramatic 1.02 Ha one), and confirmed the contrast case (sector ground
IS the global min) verifies correctly with a padded claim. Also confirmed
certkit's own producer.certify_lambda_min on the SAME defeating matrix finds
the true minimum, because _ground_state always solves the whole operator,
never a sector -- demonstrating the acceptance criterion's "full-space route"
already exists in-repo.

Root cause of why this can never become a false VERIFIED: _rule_temple_inertia
/_rule_temple_ref discharge beta by inertia-counting eigenvalues of the actual
operator the certificate references (via op.interval_rows(), independent of
whatever subspace reasoning produced beta), not the producer's sector. A
sector-local beta that fails to separate the true full spectrum makes that
count come out != 1 and the rule abstains before Temple's arithmetic runs.
This was already true of the existing code -- no rule changed.

Satisfied acceptance criterion (b): documented the invariant explicitly in
README.md ("The guarantee" item 3, plus a new "Known limits" bullet) and in
checker.py's _temple() docstring, both pointing at the new regression test.
Did NOT implement acceptance criterion (a) (a sector-restricted claim kind) --
not needed given (b) is already mechanically enforced, and adding a claim kind
nothing in this repo produces would be speculative surface, not a fix.

description: The Operator interface (apply, row, interval_rows) was designed against dense, CSR, and Pauli sums that I chose. The solver's representation may not fit it. If row access is unavailable the Gershgorin route dies; if entries are not exactly represented the backward-error route dies.

title: Fix residualNorm's Norm instance: resolves to sup norm, not Euclidean, making temple_lower false as stated
description:

The vector norm here uses whatever `Norm` instance Lean resolves for `x : n -> R`.
Since `n -> R` is a plain Pi type (not `EuclideanSpace R n`), that instance
is `Pi.normedAddCommGroup`, i.e. the SUP norm (`Pi.norm_def`: `norm f = sup_i
norm (f i)`), not the Euclidean (L2) norm.

Confirmed directly this session with a standalone compiling proof:

  example : norm (![3, -4] : Fin 2 -> R) = 4 := by ...  -- compiles

(Euclidean norm would give 5.)

This makes `temple_lower` FALSE as literally stated, not just hard to prove:
Temple's inequality is a Euclidean/Pythagorean-orthogonality argument and
does not transfer to the sup norm. A random numerical search (n=2..5
symmetric matrices, 200000 trials) found violations in 9362 of them. Worst
recorded instance (n=3):

  A = [[-0.9648769165219759, -1.402188087930802,  1.5206317025965617],
       [-1.402188087930802,   1.3768143870166014, 0.709725052905338 ],

  x = [0.9971309379732416, -0.5632638677598112, 0.39510881419682375]
  eigenvalues ~ {-2.384230194603246, 2.0326690656276565, 2.0678243561257905}
  beta = 2.0326690656276565  (satisfies hmu_beta and hgap)
  rayleigh(A,x) ~ 1.4570550056625322
  residualNorm(A,x) ~ 1.075635924249074  (sup-norm based)
  LHS = rayleigh - residualNorm^2/(beta-rayleigh) ~ -0.5529595544496035
  inf eigenvalue ~ -2.384230194603246
  LHS exceeds the true lower bound by ~1.83 -- large, unambiguous.

sandbox-handoffs/certkit-8y2.3.md.

title: Pauli-sum fill-reducing LDLᵀ: prove the separator/treewidth lower bound
description:
certkit-ph1 session 6 (sandbox-handoffs/certkit-ph1.md, 'Session 6' section) established that the sparsity graph of a PauliSumReal operator is exactly the Cayley graph on Z_2^q generated by the distinct term bit-flip masks (diagonal Z-only terms contribute no edges). For a TFIM-shaped Hamiltonian (one X per qubit) this is the q-dimensional hypercube Q_q, whose balanced vertex separators have size C(q, q//2) ~ n/sqrt(q) -- polylog in n, not polynomial. Session 6 then measured greedy minimum-degree symbolic elimination directly and found the op-count proxy (sum of pivot-degree^2) gives ops/n^3 converging to a constant (~0.026 TFIM, ~0.08 JW two-body) across three doublings of n, with max pivot degree growing ~0.4-0.5n: i.e. the factorization stays cubic-order, only a 13-38x constant-factor win over dense.

That is a measurement, not a proof. Session 6 leaned on Harper's vertex-isoperimetric inequality for 'Hamming-layer cuts are asymptotically optimal' rather than deriving it, and only looked at Q_q plus one random JW-two-body instance up to n=4096.

WHAT TO DO: turn the measurement into a theorem. Prove a lower bound of the form -- for the mask families arising from (a) geometrically k-local qubit Hamiltonians and (b) Jordan-Wigner-mapped electronic-structure Hamiltonians, every balanced vertex separator of the generated Cayley graph on Z_2^q has size Omega(n / polylog n), hence any fill-reducing elimination order yields an LDLᵀ factor of Omega(n^{3-o(1)}) arithmetic cost. Standard tools: Cayley-graph expansion / isoperimetry on Z_2^q, treewidth lower bounds via bramble or well-linked sets, the Alon-Seymour-Thomas style separator-to-treewidth relation. The k-local case is likely the tractable half; the JW case may reduce to a stated open sub-question about the structure of the two-body mask set.

If the bound is FALSE for some useful mask family -- i.e. that family has o(n) balanced separators -- that is itself the result: hand the family to the sibling empirical bead as a candidate worth a real interval-LDLᵀ implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Either: a written proof (in the handoff; or a lean/ file if short) of an Omega(n/polylog n) balanced-separator (equivalently Omega(n/polylog n) treewidth) lower bound for the Cayley graph on Z_2^q of at least the geometrically-k-local mask family, with the JW/electronic-structure case either covered or explicitly reduced to a named open sub-question. OR: an explicit mask family with balanced vertex separators of size o(n), with the generating Hamiltonian class named, handed off as input to the empirical follow-up bead.
